title: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
summary: How extra compute per prompt improves LLM answers: pass@k, voting, verifiers and their ceilings, PRM and tree search, compute-optimal allocation, reasoning models, memory costs, and a hands-on lab.
outcomes: Compute pass@k from a per-sample success rate and with the unbiased estimator from n samples
Explain why majority vote and reward models plateau while coverage keeps rising
Predict the best-of-N ceiling from a verifier's error rates and explain when more votes lower accuracy
Choose between best-of-N, PRM beam search, revisions and tree search based on prompt difficulty and evaluator quality
Trace MCTS with UCT on a small reasoning tree and compare search methods at equal compute
Explain how reasoning models and s1 budget forcing turn thinking tokens into accuracy, and where it stops or reverses
Compute the FLOPs-matched test-time budget versus a larger model and explain how KV-cache traffic changes the answer
Measure pass@k and majority-vote curves from your own samples and read the coverage-versus-selection gap

lessons.title: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt

blocks.md: Scaling laws describe how loss falls as you spend more **training** compute: more parameters, more tokens. But once a model is trained, we usually let it answer each prompt **once**, with one pass of decoding. **Test-time compute** (also called inference-time compute) is everything extra you spend on a single prompt after training: more samples, longer reasoning, or a search guided by a scorer.

Why would that help? A model that answers a hard math problem correctly 20% of the time already *contains* the solution in its output distribution. One greedy answer throws that away. **Greedy decoding** always takes the single most likely next token, so the same prompt gives the same answer every time. **Sampling** instead draws each token at random from the model's probabilities. The **temperature** $T$ divides the model's token scores before they are turned into probabilities: $T$ near 0 approaches greedy, and a higher $T$ spreads the choices, so repeated samples differ. Sampling many times, thinking longer, or revising can recover that correct answer. The question this course answers is how far that goes and how to spend the extra compute well.

Snell et al. (UC Berkeley and Google DeepMind, 2024) give a useful frame. Test-time methods have two parts:

- a **proposer**: the LLM's distribution over answers, which you can improve at test time (for example by asking it to revise its own previous attempts), and
- a **verifier**: anything that scores or selects among candidates (unit tests, a proof checker, a majority vote, an outcome reward model, or a process reward model). A **reward model** is a trained scorer: an outcome reward model scores a finished answer, a process reward model each reasoning step.

The s1 paper (*s1: Simple test-time scaling*, Muennighoff et al., 2025), citing Snell et al. and Brown et al., names a second split: **parallel** methods run independent attempts (**best-of-N**: sample $N$ answers and keep the one a verifier scores highest; **majority voting**: keep the most common final answer), while **sequential** methods let later computation build on earlier computation (a longer **chain of thought**, the step-by-step reasoning a model writes before its final answer, or revisions).

blocks.title: Proposer and verifier, parallel and sequential

scenes.caption: The default: one prompt, one pass through the model, one answer. All the model's other possible answers are never seen.
Parallel scaling: draw N independent samples at positive temperature. They can explore different approaches, but none of them learns from the others.
A verifier turns many samples into one answer. Its quality decides whether the extra samples help at all.
Sequential scaling: each new attempt conditions on the previous ones (a revision, or simply more chain of thought), so it can fix a mistake instead of starting over.
Snell et al. mix both: some budget on parallel chains, some on revising within each chain, with the verifier picking within and across chains.

blocks.md: To compare methods fairly we need a unit of cost. Papers usually count **generations** (one full sampled answer), **tokens**, or **FLOPs** (each one multiply or one add of two numbers). A rough rule from the scaling-laws literature, used by Snell et al., is that generating $D$ tokens with an $N$-parameter dense model costs about $2ND$ FLOPs, while training on $D$ tokens costs about $6ND$. Here $N$ counts parameters, not samples, and *dense* means every parameter is used for every token. The 2 comes from each parameter taking part in one multiply and one add per token on the forward pass; training adds a backward pass that costs about twice the forward pass, so $2 + 4 = 6$. We return to that exchange rate in lesson 8.

Test-time scaling has two halves that can fail independently. **Coverage**: does any attempt contain a correct answer? **Precision**: can you pick it out? The next two lessons take them one at a time.

Test-time compute is not free at serving time. Every extra sample or thinking token is paid on every request, by every user. Training compute is paid once. That asymmetry decides when test-time scaling is worth it.

blocks.question: A team samples 16 answers per question from a fixed model and keeps the one their reward model scores highest. In the proposer/verifier frame, what are they changing?
options: Only the verifier side: the proposal distribution is the same model sampled 16 times
Only the proposer: more samples means a better model
Both, because sampling at temperature changes the model's weights
Neither: this is training-time compute
blocks.explain: Best-of-N leaves the proposer untouched; each of the 16 samples comes from the same distribution. All the gain comes from selecting among them with a verifier. Changing the proposer means, for example, conditioning on previous attempts (revisions) or a longer reasoning trace.

blocks.question: Which method is **sequential** in the s1 paper's sense?
options: Majority vote over 64 independent samples
Best-of-N with unit tests
Letting the model keep reasoning after it tried to stop, so later tokens build on earlier ones
Running the same prompt on 8 GPUs at once
blocks.explain: Sequential means later computation depends on earlier computation, like a longer chain of thought or a revision. The other options are independent attempts (parallel) or just hardware parallelism.

lessons.title: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples

blocks.md: Start with one problem. Suppose each independent sample is correct with probability $p$ (the model's **per-sample success rate**, also called pass@1 for that problem). If we draw $k$ samples, the chance that **at least one** is correct is one minus the chance that all $k$ fail.

blocks.caption: Assumes the k samples are independent draws with the same success rate p.

blocks.md: A tiny example. With $p = 0.05$: one sample succeeds 5% of the time, 10 samples succeed $1 - 0.95^{10} = 40.1\%$ of the time, 50 samples 92.3%, and 100 samples 99.4%. You need 45 samples to pass 90%. A model that looks useless with one shot can be very useful if something can check its answers.

blocks.title: pass@k for one problem with per-sample success rate p

scenes.caption: p = 0.05: 5% at k = 1, 40.1% at k = 10, 99.4% at k = 100. On a log x-axis each curve is an S shape.
An easier problem (p = 0.3) saturates by k of about 10. A harder one (p = 0.02) needs about 100 samples to reach 87%.
Drag p. Every curve has the same shape, just shifted left or right on the log axis: halving p roughly doubles the k needed.

blocks.md: A benchmark is many problems with very different $p$. **Coverage** (Brown et al., 2024, *Large Language Monkeys*) is the fraction of problems solved by at least one of $k$ samples: the average of pass@k over problems. Averaging S-curves with offsets spread over orders of magnitude gives a curve that rises steadily over many decades of $k$.

blocks.title: Coverage of a 4-problem benchmark (p = 0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001)

scenes.caption: At k = 1 coverage is just mean p: (0.5 + 0.1 + 0.01 + 0.001) / 4 = 0.153.
Each 10x more samples unlocks the next harder problem: 0.439, then 0.682. The easy problem is already solved and stops contributing.
0.908 at 1,000 and 1.0 at 10,000. Gains per decade stay roughly steady (0.29, 0.24, 0.23) until the last problem is solved: this is why real coverage curves look log-linear over orders of magnitude.

blocks.md: Brown et al. measured this with up to 10,000 samples per problem. On SWE-bench Lite (real GitHub issues checked by unit tests), DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct solved 15.9% of issues with one sample and 56% with 250, above the 43% single-attempt state of the art at the time. On CodeContests (competitive programming problems from DeepMind's AlphaCode work, checked by hidden tests), Gemma-2B (the B counts billions of parameters) went from 0.02% to 7.1% coverage at 10,000 samples. On MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021: 12,500 competition math problems, each with an exact final answer), they fit coverage $c$ as an **exponentiated power law** in the number of samples $k$, with fitted constants $a$ and $b$:

blocks.caption: Brown et al., eq. 3. Taking the log, log c equals a times k to the b: with b negative that shrinks toward 0 as k grows, so coverage climbs toward 1, more slowly the more negative a is. For Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH they report a = -1.33, b = -0.43.

blocks.title: Fitted coverage law, Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH

scenes.caption: With the paper's fit, k = 100 gives 83.2% (the paper measured 82.9%) and k = 10,000 gives 97.5% (measured 98.44%).
A more negative a shifts the curve right (a weaker model needs more samples). Here a = -3.88, b = -0.11, the paper's Llama-3-8B-Instruct CodeContests fit, which climbs far more slowly.

blocks.md: When you estimate pass@k from data, do not compute $1 - (1 - \hat p)^k$ from the observed rate $\hat p$ (the fraction of samples that were correct). That curve bends, so plugging a noisy estimate into it comes out too low on average. Also do not draw just $k$ samples once (high variance). Chen et al. (2021, the Codex paper) draw $n \ge k$ samples, count $c$ correct (here $c$ is a count of correct samples, not coverage), and use the **unbiased** estimator below (unbiased: averaged over many repeats of the experiment it equals the true pass@k), the probability that a random size-$k$ subset of the $n$ samples contains at least one correct one. Brown et al. use the same formula.

blocks.caption: The fraction is the chance that all k picked samples are wrong: ways to choose all k from the n minus c wrong ones, over all ways to choose k. Code computes it as a product of factors 1 minus k over i, for i from n minus c plus 1 to n, avoiding huge binomials.

blocks.title: The numerically stable estimator from the Codex paper

scenes.caption: 10 samples, 3 correct, and we ask for pass@2.
There are 7 wrong samples, at least k = 2, so some 2-subsets can be all wrong. No early return.
The product telescopes to C(7,2)/C(10,2) = 21/45 without computing large binomials: (1 - 2/8)(1 - 2/9)(1 - 2/10) = 0.75 x 0.778 x 0.8 = 0.467.
pass@2 = 0.533. The plug-in formula 1 - 0.7^2 = 0.51 gives a different number: the estimator counts subsets of the samples you actually drew.

blocks.prompt: Same data, n = 10 and c = 3. What does the estimator give for pass@5, and how does it compare with $1 - 0.7^5$?
blocks.reveal: $1 - \binom{7}{5}/\binom{10}{5} = 1 - 21/252 = 0.917$, while $1 - 0.7^5 = 0.832$. With only 7 wrong samples, most 5-subsets must contain a correct one. The estimator is unbiased for any $n \ge k$; drawing $n$ much larger than $k$ only lowers its variance. The Codex paper used $n = 200$ for $k \le 100$ and averaged over problems.

blocks.md: Coverage is an **upper bound** on accuracy. It equals real accuracy only if you have a perfect checker (unit tests, a proof checker). For a math word problem, pass@100 = 83% means 83% of problems have *some* correct sample, not that you can find it.

blocks.question: A model has pass@1 = 0.01 on a problem. Roughly how many independent samples give a 63% chance of at least one correct answer?
options: About 10
About 63
About 100
About 1,000
blocks.explain: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. In general, $k \approx 1/p$ samples give about $1 - 1/e = 63\%$ coverage for small $p$.

blocks.question: Brown et al. find coverage on many tasks grows roughly log-linearly with k over several orders of magnitude. What best explains that shape?
options: Samples from an LLM become more accurate as you draw more of them
The benchmark mixes problems whose per-sample success rates span many orders of magnitude, so each 10x in k unlocks another slice
Temperature is raised automatically as k grows
pass@k for a single problem is linear in log k
blocks.explain: For one problem, pass@k is a sharp S-curve in log k. Averaging many such curves with offsets spread across decades smooths them into a steady rise. Samples are independent and do not get better individually.

lessons.title: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau

blocks.md:
Without an automatic checker, you must choose one answer from $N$ samples. Three standard rules:

1. **Majority vote** (self-consistency, Wang et al., 2022): parse each sample's final answer and return the most common one.
2. **Best-of-N**: score every sample with a reward model (a trained scorer) and return the top-scoring sample's answer.
3. **Weighted best-of-N**: add up reward scores for samples that share a final answer and return the answer with the largest total (used by Snell et al., following Li et al.).

Self-consistency sampled 40 reasoning paths and, on PaLM-540B (Google's 540-billion-parameter model), improved chain-of-thought accuracy on GSM8K (about 8,500 grade-school math word problems, Cobbe et al., 2021) by 17.9 points over greedy decoding.

Let us run all three rules on the same 8 samples for one problem whose correct answer is 15. Each sample has a final answer and a verifier score in [0, 1] (the score is an illustrative number, not from a real model).

blocks.title: Eight samples, three selection rules (toy scores)

scenes.caption: Eight samples. The correct answer, 15, appears twice. Wrong answer 12 appears three times.
Majority vote counts answers: 12 has 3 votes, 15 and 18 have 2, 20 has 1. It returns 12: wrong, because a wrong answer is the plurality.
Best-of-N returns the single top score, 0.92, whose answer is 20: wrong. One overconfident score decides everything.
Weighted best-of-N sums scores per answer: 15 gets 0.85 + 0.80 = 1.65, 12 gets 1.20, 20 gets 0.92, 18 gets 0.30. It returns 15: correct.

blocks.md: Weighted voting combines two weak signals: how often the model reaches an answer and how much the verifier likes it. Snell et al. adopt it, following Li et al., as the final selection step in all their PRM search experiments.

Now ask what happens as $N$ grows. Majority vote converges to whichever answer has the largest probability under the model. The answer with the largest probability is the **mode** of the distribution. If the correct answer is the mode of the model's answer distribution, accuracy climbs toward 100%. If a wrong answer is the mode, accuracy falls toward 0%, even though coverage rises to 100%. Here are exact numbers for two toy problems (ties broken at random).

blocks.prompt: Problem B: the model answers correctly with probability 0.2 and gives one particular wrong answer with probability 0.5 (the rest is split between two other wrong answers, 0.15 each). What happens to majority-vote accuracy as N goes from 1 to 64?
blocks.reveal: It **falls**: 0.20 at N = 1, 0.159 at N = 4, 0.059 at N = 16, and 0.001 at N = 64. Meanwhile coverage $1 - 0.8^N$ rises to 0.59, 0.97 and essentially 1.0. More samples make the vote more confident in the model's favorite wrong answer.

blocks.title: Majority vote vs coverage as N grows (exact, toy distributions)

scenes.caption: Problem A: correct answer has probability 0.4, wrong ones 0.3, 0.2, 0.1. Correct is the mode, so majority accuracy rises: 0.40, 0.47, 0.63, 0.83.
Problem B: correct 0.2, one wrong answer 0.5. The wrong answer is the mode, so majority accuracy drops: 0.20, 0.16, 0.06, 0.001.
Coverage on problem B over the same N: 0.20, 0.59, 0.97, 1.00. The correct answer is almost surely in the pool; voting just cannot find it.

blocks.md: This is exactly what Brown et al. observed at scale. With Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH, coverage rose from 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote and reward-model selection only moved from 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. All three selection methods plateaued around 100 samples. Rare correct answers, sampled 1% of the time or less, are a needle in a haystack that a vote cannot find and an imperfect reward model often misses. Lesson 4 turns this into a formula: when correct answers are rare, the verifier's false accepts on the many wrong samples set a ceiling that no number of samples can lift.

Reward models have a second failure: **over-optimization**. The harder you search for a high score, the more you find samples that exploit the verifier's mistakes rather than samples that are correct. Snell et al. saw this with PRM-guided search on easy questions (lesson 5). Even unit tests are imperfect: Brown et al. found flaky test suites (tests that do not give the same result each time they run on the same code) in 11.3% of SWE-bench Lite problems.
Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

blocks.question: Your majority-vote accuracy on a math benchmark stops improving between N = 64 and N = 512, but pass@512 (checked against the answer key) keeps rising. What is the most likely reason?
options: Samples become correlated at large N
On the unsolved problems the correct answer is a minority answer, so adding votes reinforces the wrong mode
The model runs out of context window
pass@k is computed incorrectly at large N
blocks.explain: Majority vote converges to the mode of the answer distribution. For problems where a wrong answer is the mode, more samples raise coverage but not voting accuracy. That is the plateau Brown et al. report.

blocks.question: With the eight toy samples above, which rule would change its answer if sample 4 (answer 20, score 0.92) were removed?
options: Majority vote
Weighted best-of-N
Best-of-N
All three
blocks.explain: Best-of-N would switch to the next-highest score, 0.85, whose answer is 15. Majority vote still picks 12 (3 votes) and weighted best-of-N still picks 15 (1.65 vs 1.20).

lessons.title: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification

blocks.md: Lesson 3 left a gap. Brown et al. saw coverage reach 98% while selection stalled near 41%, and we blamed the verifier without saying by how much. A tiny model predicts the stall. Take one hard problem where each sample is correct with probability $p = 0.05$. A **verifier** (any checker that says accept or reject) accepts a correct sample with probability $t = 0.9$, its **true positive rate**, and accepts a wrong sample with probability $f$, its **false positive rate**. The selection rule: return a random accepted sample, or a random sample if none is accepted.

blocks.caption: With many samples some sample is almost surely accepted, so the pick is a random accepted one. A sample is accepted and correct with probability p t, accepted and wrong with probability (1 minus p) f. Their ratio is the verifier's precision on this problem.

blocks.md: With $t = 0.9$: at $f = 0.01$ the ceiling is $0.045 / (0.045 + 0.0095) = 0.826$, at $f = 0.05$ it is 0.487, and at $f = 0.2$ only 0.191. Coverage meanwhile is 0.401 at $N = 10$ and 0.994 at $N = 100$. The full curve, derived step by step in the agent-verification course (optional, not a prerequisite), is $(1 - c^N)$ times the ceiling plus $c^{N-1} p (1-t)$, where $c = 1 - pt - (1-p)f$ is the chance that one sample is rejected. A lenient verifier reaches its ceiling fast (99% of it by $N = 18$ at $f = 0.2$), and every sample after that is wasted.

blocks.title: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier (p = 0.05, t = 0.9)

scenes.caption: A perfect checker turns coverage into accuracy: 0.401 at N = 10, 0.994 at N = 100.
f = 0.01: accuracy climbs to 0.823 at N = 100 and stops at the ceiling 0.826, while coverage is already 0.994.
f = 0.05 and f = 0.2 flatten at 0.487 and 0.191. With 19 wrong samples for every correct one, a few percent of false accepts swamp the correct ones.
Drag the sliders. Raising t speeds the climb but lifts the ceiling only a little (0.725 at t = 0.5, 0.840 at t = 1); lowering f or raising p (an easier problem) lifts it far more.

blocks.md: The false positive rate sets the ceiling, and it is multiplied by the number of wrong samples. At $p = 0.01$, even $t = 0.9$ and $f = 0.01$ give a ceiling of $0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0099) = 0.48$. Rare correct answers drown among rare false accepts: that is lesson 3's plateau, now as a formula.

Majority vote has its own twist. Chen et al. (2024, *Are More LLM Calls All You Need?*) study **Vote** (majority over $K$ calls) and **Filter-Vote** (an LLM filter first discards answers it judges wrong, the rest vote, and if all are discarded everything votes). Call a query **easy** if voting with unlimited calls returns the right answer, which happens when the correct answer is the most likely one (problem A in lesson 3), and **hard** otherwise (problem B). More calls push easy queries toward 100% and hard ones toward 0%, so a task that mixes the two can rise and then fall.

blocks.title: Vote on a mix: 40% easy (p = 0.8), 60% hard (p = 0.4), two answers

scenes.caption: Easy queries (the correct answer has probability 0.8): voting accuracy climbs 0.80, 0.896, 0.988, then 1.0.
Hard queries (the correct answer has probability 0.4, so the wrong one is the mode): 0.40, 0.352, 0.247, then 0.021.
The mix: 0.560, a peak of 0.570 at K = 3, then 0.543 and 0.413. Easy queries saturate early; hard ones keep sliding. Exact binomial sums, odd K so there are no ties.

blocks.md: In their experiments with GPT-3.5 on MMLU Physics, TruthfulQA, GPQA and AVeriTeC, Vote and Filter-Vote were often non-monotone in the number of calls; on MMLU Physics, Filter-Vote even went down first and then up. For two possible answers they prove when each shape appears from the two success rates and the fraction of hard queries, and they fit their scaling model from a small number of samples to predict the best number of calls. The analysis targets tasks with few possible answers, such as multiple choice.

So far a verifier was a fixed classifier. **Generative verifiers**, met in the process-reward-models course, let verification itself scale with test-time compute. GenRM (Zhang et al., 2024) trains an LLM with next-token prediction to write a verification chain of thought and then answer Yes or No; the score is the probability of Yes, averaged over $K$ sampled rationales (32 by default). That gives a second knob next to the number of samples: how much to spend checking each one. With a fixed generator, the paper reports best-of-N gains from 5% to 45.3% of problems solved on two algorithmic string tasks (Gemma-2B verifiers) and from 73% to 93.4% on GSM8K (a Gemma2-9B verifier choosing among Gemini 1.0 Pro solutions).

Zhao et al. (2025, *Sample, Scrutinize and Scale*) test the most minimal version: one model both answers and checks. It samples $k_{\text{inf}}$ responses, then scores each one $k_{\text{verif}}$ times by asking itself whether the response is correct (each check rewrites the response as a theorem with lemmas and proofs and scans it for errors), and the highest average score wins. When the top candidates score within 0.05 of each other and disagree on the answer, the model compares them in pairwise matchups, each repeated 100 times, and the most wins is returned. One problem from AIME 2024 (a hard high-school math contest with integer answers from 0 to 999) shows why this can beat voting:

blocks.title: AIME 2024 II, problem 11: 200 Gemini 1.5 Pro samples

scenes.caption: How often each final answer appeared among 200 samples (top five shown, plus 601). Majority vote returns 1, found by 124 samples. It is wrong.
Average self-verification score per answer: 0.36 for 1, 0.40, 0.52, 0.76, 0.38, and 0.98 for 601. Verification picks 601, the correct answer, found by a single sample.

blocks.title: Sampling-based search vs voting (Zhao et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: AIME 2024 Exam II (15 problems), Gemini 1.5 Pro. Voting stalls at 4 (3 with 1,000 samples); self-verification over 200 samples solves 8. Single runs, so small differences are noise.

LiveBench Reasoning (puzzles from a benchmark that adds new questions regularly to limit training-set leaks), out of 140: 63, 75, 73, then 97 with verification, against a reported 95 for o1-preview, an OpenAI reasoning model (lesson 7).

blocks.md: Two findings explain why this keeps scaling after voting saturates. **Implicit scaling**: on questions where at least one sample was correct, verification accuracy *rose* as more samples were drawn, because a larger pool is more likely to contain a rigorous, well-written correct answer that is easy to verify. **Compare to localize**: models often miss an error when checking one answer alone, but the places where two candidates disagree point to where an error may be. The price is steep. On AIME, 200 samples with 50 checks each, at about 13,000 tokens per check, is about 130M output tokens: roughly USD 650 per question at the Gemini 1.5 Pro price the authors quote, USD 200 with a cheap preliminary scoring pass, and USD 12 with Gemini 1.5 Flash as the verifier.

Self-verification is not free precision. The same paper finds that frontier models have remarkably weak verification out of the box and needed these prompting strategies (and introduces a benchmark for it). Before scaling N, measure your verifier's true and false positive rates on your own samples.

Code comes with a partial checker. AlphaCode (Li et al., 2022) could submit only 10 programs per competitive-programming problem but sampled up to a million; **10@k** is the share of problems solved with 10 submissions chosen from $k$ samples. First it **filtered**: keep only programs that pass the example tests printed in the problem statement. That removed about 99% of samples, still left thousands for many problems, and on about 10% of problems no sample passed at all. Then it **clustered**: a separately trained model wrote new test inputs, every surviving program ran on them, and programs with identical outputs formed one cluster. It submitted one program per cluster, largest first, because there are many ways to be wrong but correct programs tend to behave the same.

blocks.title: Filter, then cluster by behavior (toy, 10 programs)

scenes.caption: Ten sampled programs. Five fail the example tests from the statement and are dropped (filtering).
The five survivors run on model-generated inputs. Programs 1, 3 and 7 print identical outputs (cluster A); 6 prints B; 9 prints C. The generated inputs need not even be valid to separate behaviors.
Submit one program per cluster, largest first: A (3 programs), then B, then C. Three submissions cover all distinct behaviors instead of wasting slots on copies.

blocks.md: In AlphaCode's build-up ablation on the CodeContests validation set, adding clustering raised 10@100K from 21.5% to 24.1% and 10@1M from 24.2% to 28.4%. Still, the paper notes a large gap to the upper bound of unlimited submissions. CodeT, covered in the optional agent-verification course, goes one step further and asks the model to write the tests too, then scores groups by how many solutions and tests agree.

blocks.question: A verifier has true positive rate 0.95 and false positive rate 0.02. On a problem where 2% of samples are correct, what accuracy does best-of-N approach as N grows?
options: About 0.95, its true positive rate
About 0.98, one minus its false positive rate
About 1.0, because coverage reaches 1
About 0.49
blocks.explain: The ceiling is $pt / (pt + (1-p)f) = 0.019 / (0.019 + 0.0196) = 0.49$. Correct accepted samples and wrong accepted samples arrive at almost the same rate because wrong samples outnumber correct ones 49 to 1.

blocks.question: On a benchmark, majority-vote accuracy rises from 1 to 5 calls and then falls steadily up to 101 calls. Which explanation fits Chen et al.'s analysis?
options: The benchmark mixes queries whose most likely answer is correct, which saturate early, with queries whose most likely answer is wrong, which keep sliding toward 0
Samples become correlated when K is large
Ties are broken in favor of wrong answers
The temperature rises with K
blocks.explain: Voting converges to the mode of each query's answer distribution. Easy queries gain until they hit 100% and then stop contributing; hard queries lose with every extra call, so the average eventually turns down.

blocks.question: After filtering, AlphaCode still has 2,000 programs that pass the example tests and only 10 submissions. Why pick one program from each of the largest behavior clusters?
options: Large clusters contain the shortest programs
Clustering runs the hidden tests in advance
Programs with identical outputs are redundant submissions, and correct programs tend to agree with each other, so big clusters are more likely correct
It guarantees that one submission passes
blocks.explain: Random picks waste submissions on semantically equal programs. Grouping by behavior on new inputs spreads the 10 submissions over distinct behaviors, and the paper found that going from largest to smallest cluster worked best.

lessons.title: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation

blocks.md:
A process reward model (PRM) scores every **step** of a solution, not just the final answer. Best-of-N only uses the PRM at the end. With step scores we can **prune** bad partial solutions early and spend the budget on promising ones. Snell et al. compare three ways to search against a PRM, all at the same *generation budget* $N$:

- **Best-of-N weighted**: sample $N$ full solutions, score each by the PRM's prediction at its last step, aggregate per answer.
- **Beam search**: keep $N$ candidates; after each step keep the top $N/M$ by PRM score and expand each into $M$ new next steps.
- **Lookahead search**: beam search, but score each step by rolling it out $k$ more steps greedily (here $k$ is a lookahead depth, not a sample count) and using the PRM at the end of the rollout. A **rollout** just continues generating from that step to see where it leads. Every step is generated once plus $k$ rollout steps, so each of the $N$ beams costs $k+1$ samples, $N \times (k+1)$ in all.

blocks.title: Beam search with N = 4 candidates, M = 2 (toy PRM scores)

scenes.caption: Sample N = 4 different first steps and score each with the PRM.
Keep the top N/M = 2 (A and C). B and D are dropped after one step instead of being completed, which is where the savings come from.
Expand each survivor into M = 2 next steps: back to 4 candidates. Score again and keep A1 (.66) and C2 (.80).
Repeat until solutions finish (Snell et al. cap it at 40 rounds). Step 3 shows the children of A1 (.70, .58) and C2 (.83, .31). The finished candidates then go through weighted best-of-N.

blocks.md: What did they find on MATH with PaLM 2-S* (a small model from Google's PaLM 2 family; the star marks Google's version further trained on code)? At small budgets beam search clearly beat best-of-N. As the budget grew the advantage shrank and beam search often fell **below** best-of-N. Lookahead search, the most thorough optimizer, generally did worst at equal budget. Inspecting outputs showed the search exploiting the PRM: repetitive low-information steps, or suspiciously short 1 to 2 step solutions.

Splitting the test set by **difficulty** explains it. Snell et al. define difficulty relative to the model: estimate each question's pass@1 from 2048 samples and bin questions into five quantiles (level 1 easiest). On easy levels 1 and 2, beam search **degraded** with more budget, amplifying the PRM's spurious features where the model was already mostly right. On levels 3 and 4, beam search consistently beat best-of-N, because there the model rarely samples a correct answer without guidance. On level 5 no method made much progress.

blocks.title: A compute-optimal router (simplified from Snell et al.)

nodes.label:
Medium bins:
PRM beam search,
seq/parallel mix

Hardest bin:
little gain from
test-time compute

scenes.caption: The compute-optimal strategy picks the test-time hyperparameters (search method, beam width, sequential vs parallel ratio) per prompt, using difficulty as the deciding statistic.
In practice difficulty is predicted from the verifier's average score on samples, not from ground truth. The two versions gave largely overlapping curves in the paper.
Easy prompts: the first samples are usually near-right, so local refinement wins and aggressive search risks exploiting the verifier.
Medium prompts: guided search and a balance of parallel exploration with sequential revision pay off most.
Hardest prompts: the paper saw small gains from any method. Here a bigger or better-trained model is the lever.

blocks.md: How does the router get a difficulty without the answer key? Snell et al. bin each question by the **average final-answer score** a learned verifier gives its samples, with bins set as quintiles of that statistic over the test questions themselves (a deployed router would take the edges from earlier prompts). A worked example with 16 samples: the PRM scores the last step of each, the scores are averaged, and the average is looked up against the edges.

blocks.caption: Run here. Scores and bin edges are illustrative; in practice the edges come from held-out questions.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
# PRM score of the final step for 16 samples of one new prompt (illustrative)
s = np.array([.91, .12, .35, .88, .20, .47, .66, .15, .72, .30, .41, .09, .58, .25, .83, .38])
# bin edges: quintiles of the same statistic on held-out prompts (illustrative)
edges = [0.22, 0.38, 0.55, 0.72]        # above 0.72 is bin 1 (easiest)
v = s.mean()
b = 5 - int(np.searchsorted(edges, v))  # 1 = easiest, 5 = hardest
print(f"mean score {v:.3f}, bin {b}")
# output: mean score 0.456, bin 3

blocks.md: Bin 3 is a medium question, so the router picks PRM beam search. The estimate is not free: with a budget of 64 generations, these 16 leave 48 for search unless they are reused as candidates in the final weighted vote. Snell et al. estimated difficulty from 2048 samples per question and, for simplicity, did not count that cost in their comparisons; they note it would be a problem in production and suggest training a model to predict difficulty from the question alone.

Snell et al. also changed the **proposer**. They fine-tuned PaLM 2-S* to revise its answer given up to four previous attempts in context. Its pass@1 improved with each revision step, and generating $N$ answers as a sequence of revisions narrowly beat generating $N$ in parallel. But about 38% of correct answers were turned back into incorrect ones by a later revision, so they again used a verifier or majority vote to pick the best answer in each chain. Easy questions did best with all-sequential compute; harder ones with a mix of sequential and parallel.

Choosing the best setting per difficulty bin (on held-out data) is what they call **compute-optimal scaling**. With PRM search it nearly matched best-of-N while using up to 4x less compute (16 versus 64 generations); with revisions it outperformed best-of-N using up to 4x less (64 versus 256). In the discussion they summarize the efficiency gain as 2x to 4x.

These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.
The best use of test-time compute depends on the prompt. Search is most valuable where the model is weak but not hopeless; on easy prompts it can hurt by exploiting the verifier.

blocks.question: Beam search with a PRM beats best-of-N at 16 generations but loses at 256 on easy questions. What is the best explanation?
options: Beam search runs out of beams at large N
With more budget the search finds candidates that score high because of PRM errors, not because they are correct
Best-of-N uses a better reward model
Easy questions need more steps than beam search allows
blocks.explain: This is verifier over-optimization. Snell et al. saw search produce repetitive or overly short solutions that the PRM still scored well. On easy questions best-of-N's weaker optimization pressure is safer.

blocks.question: Lookahead search with k = 3 and N = 16 beams is charged how many generations in Snell et al.'s cost protocol?
blocks.explain: Lookahead costs N x (k + 1) = 16 x 4 = 64, because each step is also rolled out k steps ahead. That extra cost is one reason it underperformed at equal budget.

blocks.question: A product mostly receives easy prompts that the model already solves 70% of the time. Which allocation does the paper's evidence favor?
options: Deep lookahead search against a PRM
Spend the budget sequentially (revise or keep reasoning) rather than on aggressive PRM search
Skip any verifier and return the first sample
Always use the maximum number of parallel samples
blocks.explain: On easy bins, sequential revisions did best and beam search degraded with budget. Light selection (vote or weighted best-of-N) over a revision chain is the safer choice.

lessons.title: Tree search for reasoning: Tree of Thoughts, MCTS, inference laws

blocks.md: **Game of 24**: combine four numbers with $+$, $-$, $\times$ and $\div$, each number used once, to make 24. From 4 9 10 13 one solution is $13 - 9 = 4$ (left 4 4 10), then $10 - 4 = 6$ (left 4 6), then $4 \times 6 = 24$. The first step decides a lot: Yao et al. (2023) found that about 60% of GPT-4's chain-of-thought samples had already failed after the first step. Left-to-right decoding cannot take a step back. Beam search against a PRM (last lesson) prunes partial solutions but never returns to one it dropped. This lesson covers search that can.

blocks.title: ToT breadth-first search on 4 9 10 13 (b = 2 here; the paper used 5)

scenes.caption: The propose prompt suggests five first steps. Each leaves three numbers.
The evaluator rates each state (verdicts illustrative). 10 13 13, 9 13 40 and 4 10 22 cannot reach 24 (checked by brute force), so impossible; 4 4 10 and 6 9 13 can.
BFS keeps the best b = 2 states and expands only those. Three of five branches are never extended, which is where ToT saves tokens.
Both surviving branches reach 4 and 6, and the last step finds 4 x 6 = 24. One plain chain of thought that started with 4 + 9 would have been dead from the first token onward.

blocks.title: Game of 24, 100 hard games, GPT-4 (Yao et al., Table 2)

scenes.caption: Direct answers (IO), chain of thought and self-consistency over 100 chains solve 7.3%, 4.0% and 9.0%. Voting cannot help when most chains die at step one.
ToT with breadth 1 already solves 45%; breadth 5 solves 74%.
Even counting a CoT success if any of 100 samples is right (an oracle, like pass@100) gives 49%. ToT used about 5.5k completion tokens per game versus 6.7k for those 100 chains.

blocks.md:
ToT's BFS judges each state once. **Monte Carlo tree search** (MCTS), the search behind AlphaGo, keeps running statistics and revisits nodes. Every node $s$ stores a visit count $N(s)$ and a total result $q(s)$, so its average is $Q(s) = q(s)/N(s)$. Each iteration has four phases:

1. **Selection**: from the root, repeatedly move to the child with the highest UCT score, until reaching a node with a child not yet added.
2. **Expansion**: add one new child (one sampled next step).
3. **Evaluation**: score it, with a **rollout** (finish the solution and check the answer) or with a PRM.
4. **Backup**: add the result to $q$ and 1 to $N$ for every node on the path.

blocks.caption: UCT (Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees, Kocsis and Szepesvari), in the form rStar-Math writes it. The first term favors nodes that did well (exploit); the second grows for nodes visited rarely relative to their parent (explore); c trades them off. Unvisited children are tried first.

blocks.title: Eight MCTS iterations on a depth-3 tree (c = 1, results +1 or -1)

scenes.caption: Iterations 1 and 2: both first steps are unvisited, so both are tried. A's rollout ends in a correct answer (+1), B's in a wrong one (-1). Depth 3 is the checked answer under each step-2 node.
Iteration 3: UCT(A) = 1 + sqrt(ln 2 / 1) = 1.83, UCT(B) = -1 + 0.83 = -0.17. Select A, expand A1, whose answer checks out: +1 backed up through A and the root.
Iteration 4: UCT(A) = 1 + sqrt(ln 3 / 2) = 1.74 beats UCT(B) = 0.05. A still has an untried child, so expand A2: wrong, -1. A's average drops to 0.33.
Iteration 5: at the root A scores 1.01 and B 0.18; inside A, A1 scores 2.05 and A2 0.05. A1 is revisited and returns +1 again.

After 8 iterations: A visited 7 times (Q 0.71), A1 5 times. B still has 1 visit (Q -1.0, UCT 0.44 versus A's 1.26), so B2, also a right answer, was never tried. The answer returned is the most visited path, A then A1.

blocks.prompt: In the trace, step B was visited once (its single rollout failed) and its child B2, a correct answer, was never tried. What would make the search revisit B?
blocks.reveal: B's average is -1 while A's is 0.71. B's exploration bonus grows only with the log of the root's visits: after 8 iterations it is $\sqrt{\ln 8 / 1} = 1.44$, giving $-1 + 1.44 = 0.44$ against A's 1.26. With $c = 2$ (rStar-Math's setting when generating training data) the same tree revisits B at iteration 9. A single noisy evaluation can bury a good branch; a larger c, more iterations, or a better evaluator than one rollout (such as a PRM) counters that.

blocks.md: **rStar-Math** (Guan et al., 2025) runs MCTS over math steps with two small models: a policy that proposes steps and a **process preference model** (PPM) that scores them. Each step is natural-language reasoning plus Python code, and a candidate survives only if its code, run after all earlier steps' code, executes. To make training data, final answers are checked against ground truth and backed up as +1 or -1 (the first two rounds use no PPM at all); the PPM is trained on pairs of high-Q and low-Q steps from the trees rather than on raw Q values. Four rounds of self-evolution alternate search, retraining the policy and retraining the PPM. At test time it samples 32 candidates per step, runs 4 rollouts per step and returns the trajectory the PPM scores highest. With 64 trajectories, Qwen2.5-Math-7B went from 58.8% to 90.0% on MATH.

The same search serves twice in rStar-Math: at test time to answer, and at training time to produce verified step-by-step trajectories that the next round's policy and PPM learn from. Search spends compute once to make data that makes every later answer cheaper.

Search is not free, and fair comparisons count compute. Wu et al. (2024, *Inference Scaling Laws*) compared greedy decoding, majority voting, best-of-n, weighted voting and tree search at matched FLOPs on GSM8K and MATH500, across Pythia, Mistral-7B and Llemma-7B and 34B. Classic MCTS did *worse* than plain sampling at every budget: many of its paths exist only to estimate node values and never become candidates, and it leaves many solutions unfinished, so weighted voting gets fewer votes. Their **REBASE** (REward BAlanced SEarch) drops rollouts: a PRM scores every node at the current depth, and the remaining sampling budget is split among the nodes by a softmax of their rewards.

blocks.caption: W_j is how many children node j gets. B_i is the budget left at depth i: N minus the solutions already completed. The balance temperature T_b sets how greedy the split is; Wu et al. used T_b = 0.1.

blocks.title: REBASE splits a budget of 8 among 4 nodes (PRM rewards .9 .6 .5 .2)

scenes.caption: T_b = 0.1: the softmax gives 7.48, 0.37, 0.14, 0.01, rounded to 7, 0, 0, 0. Nearly greedy: one node gets everything, and rounding drops one sample.
T_b = 0.2: 5.76, 1.29, 0.78, 0.17, rounded to 6, 1, 1, 0. The best node dominates, but two others stay alive.
T_b = 0.5: 3.56, 1.96, 1.60, 0.88, rounded to 4, 2, 2, 1. Broad exploration; rounding overshoots the budget by one here.

blocks.title: MATH500 with weighted voting (Wu et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: Accuracy (%) for Llemma-7B and Llemma-34B: 45.5, 46.8, 46.7, 49.2. The 7B model with REBASE edges past the 34B model with plain sampling.
Inference FLOPs per question, in units of 10 to the 14: 10.0, 1.48, 12.1, 7.08. The 7B REBASE run used about 8x less compute than 34B sampling and about 7x less than 7B sampling.

blocks.md: Their broader picture: for each model, accuracy rises with inference compute and then saturates, because sampling and voting converge to a limit set by the model's own answer probabilities. Smaller models are compute-optimal at small budgets; larger ones win only once the smaller model has saturated (on MATH, Llemma-7B led Llemma-34B until 128 Llemma-7B samples). REBASE's advantage over sampling showed up on MATH levels 3 to 5; on levels 1 and 2 the two were comparable, matching lesson 5's finding that search pays on harder questions.

Tree search pays when you have a step-level evaluator you can trust (code that runs, a checked answer, a strong PRM) and when early mistakes are expensive, as in Game of 24. With a weak evaluator, more search mostly finds the evaluator's mistakes, the over-optimization seen in lesson 5. And always compare at equal compute: rollouts are not free.

blocks.question: Wu et al. found classic MCTS below plain sampling at every FLOPs budget, while REBASE was above it. What does REBASE skip that MCTS pays for?
options: Rollouts that only estimate node values and never become candidate solutions
The process reward model
The weighted vote at the end
Sampling at positive temperature
blocks.explain: REBASE scores nodes with the PRM directly and spends the whole budget on expanding nodes into candidates. MCTS spends many generations estimating values and leaves many solutions unfinished, which also weakens the final weighted vote.

blocks.question: In UCT, node X was visited once with result -1, and its sibling averages +0.7 over 7 visits. Which change makes the search revisit X soonest?
options: Lower c to 0.5
Evaluate with greedy rollouts instead of sampled ones
Stop backing results up to the root
Raise c, which scales the bonus for rarely visited nodes
blocks.explain: The exploration term is c times the square root of ln N_parent over N(X). With N(X) = 1 it is the only thing that can lift X above a sibling with a good average, and a larger c lifts it sooner.

lessons.title: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing

blocks.md: The methods so far bolt search onto an ordinary model. Reasoning models move test-time scaling **inside** one generation: the model writes a long chain of thought, checks itself, backtracks, and only then answers. OpenAI's o1 system card (the document a lab publishes on a model's training and safety testing) states that the o1 series is trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using chain of thought, and that o-series models gain capability by leveraging test-time compute. ChatGPT shows users a summary of that chain of thought rather than the raw text.

DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) published how such behavior can emerge. Recall from the grpo-rlvr course: in reinforcement learning (RL) the model is the **policy**, and GRPO updates it by sampling a group of answers to each prompt and scoring each one against the group's average reward, with no separate value model.

DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with GRPO from a **base model** (pretrained only, never tuned to follow instructions) using rule-based rewards (answer correctness and a format that puts reasoning inside `<think>` tags), with no human-written reasoning traces. Over training, its average pass@1 on AIME 2024 (both 2024 exams, 30 problems; the contest was introduced in lesson 4) rose from 15.6% to 77.9% (86.7% with self-consistency voting), and the average response length grew steadily: the model learned on its own to spend more tokens thinking. Part of that growth may be an artifact of the loss: GRPO divides each answer's loss by its length, so long wrong answers are pushed down less per token. Lesson 7 of the grpo-rlvr course explains this length bias and the Dr. GRPO fix. The paper also notes that R1 uses fewer tokens on simple tasks and more on complex ones.

Notice the two scaling knobs here. Train-time RL compute makes the model *able* to use long reasoning; test-time tokens are where it *spends* that ability on each prompt. Recall from the grpo-rlvr course that this ability has a limit: Yue et al. (2025) found RL-trained models beat their base models at pass@1, but the base models had higher pass@k at large k.

Can you control how long such a model thinks? **s1** (Muennighoff et al., 2025) shows a very simple recipe. Fine-tune Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on just 1,000 curated questions with reasoning traces (s1K), which took 26 minutes on 16 H100 GPUs. The model writes its thinking first and closes it with an **end-of-thinking delimiter**, a special token after which it gives the answer. Then apply **budget forcing** at decoding time:

- **Maximum**: if thinking exceeds the budget, append the end-of-thinking delimiter (optionally with "Final Answer:") so the model must answer now.
- **Minimum**: if the model tries to stop early, suppress the end-of-thinking delimiter and append "Wait", which often makes it re-check and fix its answer.

blocks.title: Budget forcing as a decoding loop (simplified)

scenes.caption: Decode the thinking trace one token at a time, as usual.
The model emits end-of-thinking after 900 tokens, but the minimum is 2,000. Instead of stopping, the stop token is dropped and "Wait" is appended.
Thinking continues and the model often re-examines its last step. In the s1 paper's example it recounts and fixes an answer of 2 r's in "raspberry" to 3.
If the trace hits the maximum, thinking is cut and the model is pushed straight to its answer.
Either way the answer is produced after the end-of-thinking delimiter, so test-time compute is controlled exactly by the two budgets.

blocks.md: Results: s1-32B with budget forcing scaled with more thinking tokens. Forcing it to continue (appending "Wait" up to six times) raised AIME24 from 50% to 57%, beyond what it achieved without intervention. The choice of string mattered a little: with 2 forced continuations, "Wait" gave 53.3% on AIME24 versus 50.0% for no string, "Hmm" or "Alternatively". Simply telling the model a token limit in the prompt failed, because the model cannot reliably count tokens; asking for a number of steps was gamed by writing fewer, longer steps.

blocks.prompt: s1 also tried **rejection sampling**: sample until a generation happens to fit a chosen length budget, then use it. If you raise the budget, should accuracy go up like budget forcing?
blocks.reveal: No. The authors found an **inverse** trend: longer accepted generations were less accurate. Their hypothesis: short generations are the ones where the model was on the right track from the start, and long ones are where it made mistakes and backtracked. Length is partly a *symptom* of difficulty, so filtering for length is not the same as granting more thinking.

blocks.md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window (the most tokens the model can read and write in one pass) caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

Longer can also be worse. Gema et al. (2025, *Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute*) built tasks where frontier reasoning models get less accurate as their reasoning grows: counting with distractors (*You have an apple and an orange ... there is 61% probability that they are exactly a Red Delicious apple and a Navel orange. Calculate how many fruits you have*; the answer is 2), regression on student records with spurious features, and zebra-style deduction puzzles with many clues. The failure modes differed by model family: Claude models grew more distracted by irrelevant information, OpenAI o-series models resisted distractors but overfit to familiar problem framings, models drifted from sensible priors to spurious correlations, and all of them lost track in long deductions.

Do not assume more thinking tokens never hurt. Evaluate a reasoning model at several reasoning lengths on your own tasks. Wasted tokens on easy prompts (overthinking) and how to train them away are the subject of the efficient-reasoning course, a follow-on to this one.

Sequential thinking lets later tokens build on earlier ones, which parallel sampling cannot. s1 found that majority voting over the base model could not catch up with the budget-forced fine-tuned model.

blocks.question: You fine-tuned a model like s1 and force 10 extra "Wait" continuations on every hard problem. Accuracy drops compared with 4. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model forgot its fine-tuning
Too many suppressed stops push it into repetitive loops or past the context window, so extra tokens stop adding useful reasoning
Appending "Wait" changes the model's weights
Budget forcing only works on easy problems
blocks.explain: s1 reports that scaling with budget forcing flattens and that suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter too often leads to repetitive loops, while the context window bounds total length.

blocks.question: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's responses became much longer during RL even though no reward term asked for length. Why is that evidence for test-time scaling?
options: Longer outputs are always rewarded by GRPO
Length was capped at 1,000 tokens
The model copied long human traces
The reward was only for correctness and format, so the model discovered that spending more tokens per problem raised its success rate
blocks.explain: R1-Zero's rewards were rule-based accuracy and format rewards. Growth in thinking length alongside accuracy shows the policy learned to buy correctness with test-time tokens.

lessons.title: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model

blocks.md: If extra inference can lift a small model, when is it better than training a bigger one? Snell et al. pose it with FLOPs. A model with $N$ parameters pretrained on $D_{\text{pretrain}}$ tokens costs $X = 6ND_{\text{pretrain}}$, and serving $D_{\text{inference}}$ tokens costs $Y = 2ND_{\text{inference}}$. Multiplying parameters by $M$ (same data) multiplies both, to $M(X+Y)$. To match that total with the small model, its inference compute can grow by a factor

blocks.caption: The big model costs M X plus M Y. The small model keeps X and can raise its inference to M Y plus (M minus 1) X, spending the training it saved. Divide by Y and use X over Y equals 3 over R, where R is inference tokens over pretraining tokens: M plus 3 times (M minus 1) over R.

blocks.md: Worked example with the paper's $M \approx 14$ (a 14x larger model): at $R = 0.16$ the small model may spend $14 + 3 \cdot 13 / 0.16 = 257.75$ times its baseline inference compute; at $R = 0.79$, 63.4 times; at $R = 22$, only 15.8 times. The more inference traffic you expect relative to pretraining data, the less test-time budget each query gets, because the bigger model's training cost is amortized over many queries.

blocks.title: Test-time budget that matches an M-times larger model

scenes.caption: With M = 14, the three R values Snell et al. tested give 258x, 63x and 16x more inference for the small model.
As R grows the multiplier falls toward M itself: with heavy traffic, the small model can afford barely more than the big model's per-query cost.
Drag M. A smaller gap in size (M = 4) leaves much less room: 60x at R = 0.16, under 5x at R = 22.

blocks.md: Their finding (Figure 9): test-time compute and pretraining are **not 1-to-1 exchangeable**. On easy and medium questions, or when $R$ is small (for example a self-improvement pipeline that generates few tokens), compute-optimal test-time scaling of the small model beat the 14x larger model's greedy answer. On the hardest questions, or with large $R$, scaling parameters was better. Brown et al. saw the same task dependence for repeated sampling: at fixed FLOPs, Llama-3-8B-Instruct reached higher coverage than Llama-3-70B-Instruct on MATH, GSM8K and MiniF2F (olympiad-level math statements written in a formal language, so a proof checker verifies each proof), while the 70B model was almost always more cost-effective on CodeContests.

FLOPs are not the only cost. Brown et al. note that repeated sampling can run at high batch sizes and use attention optimizations that exploit the shared prompt (all samples reuse one computation of the prompt's attention state), so its real throughput is better than FLOPs suggest. Long sequential traces have the opposite problem: tokens come out one after another, which adds latency. Brown et al. also compared API prices on SWE-bench Lite (300 issues) with the same agent framework:

blocks.title: SWE-bench Lite: solve rate and API cost (Brown et al.)

scenes.caption: Issues solved (%): five samples from the cheaper model solve 29.62%, versus 24.00% and 26.70% for one attempt from the frontier models.
Total cost in USD: 5 x 0.0072 x 300 = 10.8, versus 39 and 51. Repeated sampling is 3.6x and 4.7x cheaper here while solving more.

blocks.md: FLOPs also miss memory. Decoding is **memory-bound**: each new token needs little arithmetic, but the GPU must read all the weights plus that sequence's whole KV cache (the stored keys and values of every earlier token; the optional llm-inference-kv-cache course does the full accounting). In a batch the weight reads are shared by every sequence, but each sample reads its own KV cache, and that cache grows with every token. Kinetics (Sadhukhan et al., 2025) adds memory access to the cost model and finds that for long chains of thought, attention, not the parameters, dominates: past 4,096 generated tokens, attention-related cost exceeds parameter cost by 10 to 1,000 times.

blocks.title: Bytes read per decoding step, bf16, 32K tokens of context per sample

scenes.caption: Qwen3-0.6B, one sample: 28 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 dims x 2 (K and V) x 2 bytes = 112 KiB per token, so 3.76 GB (3.5 GiB) of KV against 1.19 GB of weights (596M unique parameters). Kinetics reports 3.5GB and 1.2GB.
Qwen3-32B, one sample: 64 layers give 256 KiB per token, 8.6 GB at 32K, against 65.5 GB of weights. The big model's KV is small relative to its size.

Qwen3-8B with 16 parallel samples: 16.4 GB of weights read once per step, but 16 x 4.83 = 77.3 GB of KV cache. A shared prompt's KV can be read once, but each sample's own tokens cannot: best-of-N multiplies what FLOPs ignore.

blocks.title: When does KV traffic pass weight traffic? (bf16, per decoding step)

scenes.caption: One sample. Qwen3-0.6B's KV reads pass its weight reads at about 10K tokens of context; Qwen3-32B's not until about 250K, beyond its native context.
16 samples: the crossover falls to about 650 tokens for 0.6B (off the left edge) and 15.6K for 32B. Long traces and many samples make every model memory-bound on attention.

blocks.md: Kinetics' conclusions on Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B on AIME: FLOPs-only scaling laws overestimate small models; compute is best spent first on model size, up to about 14B, before investing in best-of-N or longer chains; and the 0.6B model is on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier only where accuracy is negligible. One reason is that KV size grows slowly with parameters (doubling Qwen3's parameters raises KV per token only 1.18x), so small models pay relatively more for memory. With DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models the threshold was 7B. Read FLOPs-matched comparisons with this in mind, including the exchange rate above and lesson 6's finding that small models with more inference are compute-optimal at small budgets.

Putting the course together, a practical checklist:

1. **Is there a reliable checker?** (tests, proof checker, exact answer) Then repeated sampling turns coverage into accuracy, and pass@k guides the budget.
2. **No checker?** Expect majority vote and reward models to plateau; weighted voting and a good PRM help, but beware over-optimization.
3. **Difficulty varies?** Spend adaptively: little on easy prompts, guided search on medium ones, and do not expect miracles on prompts far beyond the model.
4. **Reasoning model?** Control thinking length (budget forcing or the provider's effort settings), and combine with parallel sampling once sequential gains flatten.
5. **Heavy traffic?** A bigger or better-trained model may be cheaper overall than a big per-query test-time budget.
6. **Long traces or many samples?** Count memory traffic, not only FLOPs: KV-cache reads can dominate the cost.
Test-time compute is a second scaling axis, not a replacement for the first. It pays most when the model can already sometimes solve the task and something can recognize a correct answer.

blocks.question: Using Snell et al.'s FLOPs model with M = 14, how much more inference compute can the small model use at R = 1?
A chatbot will serve far more tokens than its pretraining corpus (R much greater than 1), and many prompts are hard for the current model. What does the evidence favor?
options: Investing in a larger or better-trained model
A large per-query test-time budget on the current small model
Majority voting with 10,000 samples
Lookahead search with a PRM
blocks.explain: With large R the FLOPs-matched test-time budget shrinks toward M, and on hard questions Snell et al. found additional pretraining more effective than test-time compute.

blocks.question: Brown et al.'s DeepSeek-Coder setup beat single attempts from GPT-4o and Claude on SWE-bench Lite. Which ingredient made the extra samples convertible into solved issues?
options: A majority vote over patches
A larger context window
A process reward model
The repository's unit tests, which check each candidate automatically
blocks.explain: SWE-bench candidates are checked by the repository's test suite, so higher coverage becomes a higher solve rate directly. Without such a checker, selection plateaus, as lesson 3 showed.

lessons.title: Measure it yourself: a test-time scaling harness on GSM8K

blocks.md: Every claim in this course came from reading curves. Now produce your own. The plan: draw 64 samples for each of 200 GSM8K test questions from a small open model, parse the final answers, then compute pass@k and majority-vote accuracy for $k$ from 1 to 64 and split the questions by difficulty. The process-reward-models course already ran the verifier half of this with the same model on the first 100 of these questions (with a different, step-by-step prompt): with 16 samples per question, majority vote reached 46% and PRM-weighted voting 47% to 53%, against 79% for any of 16 right. Here we skip the reward model and look at how coverage and voting scale with $k$.

blocks.caption: Sampling, run here on an Apple Silicon laptop GPU (PyTorch MPS) with Hugging Face Transformers: 20 minutes for 200 questions x 64 samples. The 0.5B model's weights take about 1 GB in 16-bit.
blocks.code:
import json, torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL, padding_side="left")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL, dtype=torch.float16).to("mps").eval()
torch.manual_seed(0)
SYS = "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \\boxed{}."
gsm = load_dataset("openai/gsm8k", "main", split="test")
with open("samples.jsonl", "w") as out:
    for i in range(200):
        q, a = gsm[i]["question"], gsm[i]["answer"]
        msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": SYS}, {"role": "user", "content": q}]
        text = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
        enc = tok([text], return_tensors="pt").to("mps")
        with torch.no_grad():
            gen = model.generate(**enc, do_sample=True, temperature=0.8, top_p=1.0, top_k=0,
                                 repetition_penalty=1.0, num_return_sequences=64,
                                 max_new_tokens=400, pad_token_id=tok.eos_token_id)
        sols = tok.batch_decode(gen[:, enc["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)
        ref = a.split("####")[-1].strip().replace(",", "")
        out.write(json.dumps({"ref": ref, "samples": sols}) + "\n")

blocks.md: A trap we hit. Both Transformers and vLLM apply the model's `generation_config.json` by default, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct's sets temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20 and a repetition penalty of 1.1. Our first run silently kept the repetition penalty, which is not plain temperature sampling. Override every sampling setting explicitly, as above.

blocks.caption: The same sampling on an NVIDIA GPU with vLLM. Not run here (no CUDA GPU on this machine). n = 64 decodes 64 continuations of one prompt, and automatic prefix caching reuses the prompt's KV cache instead of recomputing it.
blocks.code:
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", generation_config="vllm",
          enable_prefix_caching=True)
params = SamplingParams(n=64, temperature=0.8, top_p=1.0, max_tokens=400, seed=0)
tok = llm.get_tokenizer()
prompts = [tok.apply_chat_template(msgs(q), tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
           for q in questions]          # msgs() builds the same system + user turns
outs = llm.generate(prompts, params)
samples = [[o.text for o in out.outputs] for out in outs]

blocks.md: Two estimators turn the samples into curves. **pass@k** uses the unbiased formula from lesson 2 on all 64 samples. **majority@k** has no closed form, so it is estimated: draw 200 random subsets of size $k$ from the 64, vote within each (a tie counts as a fraction: one third correct if three answers tie and one is right), and average. An answer is the last `boxed` expression, or else the last number; it is correct if it equals the reference as a number.

blocks.caption: The analysis core (the full script is about 50 lines with parsing and printing).
blocks.code:
import random
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

def pass_at_k(n, c, k):                      # Chen et al. 2021
    if n - c < k:
        return 1.0
    return 1.0 - np.prod(1.0 - k / np.arange(n - c + 1, n + 1))

def majority_at_k(answers, ref, k, trials=200, rng=random.Random(0)):
    hits = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        votes = Counter(a for a in rng.sample(answers, k) if a is not None)
        if not votes:
            continue
        top = max(votes.values())
        winners = [a for a, v in votes.items() if v == top]
        hits += sum(w == ref for w in winners) / len(winners)   # random tie-break
    return hits / trials

blocks.title: Our run: 200 GSM8K questions, 64 samples each, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct

scenes.caption: pass@k (some sample right): 0.409 at k = 1, 0.749 at k = 8, 0.935 at k = 64. Each doubling of k adds less, the averaged S-curves of lesson 2.
Majority vote: 0.408 at k = 1, 0.540 at k = 8, 0.610 at k = 64. It gains early, then flattens.

The gap, pass@k minus majority@k: 0.209 at k = 8 and 0.325 at k = 64. These are questions where a right answer was sampled but was not the most common one. Only better selection, such as a verifier, can recover them.

blocks.md: Now the difficulty split. Estimating difficulty and measuring on the same samples would bias both, so samples 1 to 32 of each question estimate its per-sample success rate, the questions are sorted into five bins of 40 (bin 1 easiest), and samples 33 to 64 measure pass@k and majority@k with $k$ up to 32. This is the oracle-difficulty setup of Snell et al. at a tiny scale; they also used cross-validation for the same reason.

blocks.prompt: Before you look: in which difficulty bins will majority vote over 32 samples gain the most over a single sample, and where will it gain nothing or even lose?
blocks.reveal: Most in the middle bins. With 32 held-out samples, majority vote beats a single sample by 0.08 in bin 1 (already 0.92, nothing left to gain), by 0.34 in bin 2 and 0.41 in bin 3, but by only 0.09 and 0.07 in bins 4 and 5. In the hard bins the correct answer is usually not the most common one, so voting has little to amplify, even though coverage there is high.

blocks.title: Per difficulty bin, held-out samples 33 to 64

scenes.caption: One sample (pass@1 on the held-out half): 0.920, 0.645, 0.294, 0.114, 0.041. The bins spread per-sample success from near certain to near hopeless.
Majority vote over 32 samples: 1.000, 0.988, 0.700, 0.200, 0.113. Bins 2 and 3 gain the most; bins 4 and 5 barely move.
pass@32: 1.000, 1.000, 1.000, 0.925, 0.575. In bin 4, 92.5% of questions have a right answer among 32 samples, yet voting finds it for 20%. That gap is the verifier's job.

blocks.md: This is Snell et al.'s qualitative picture at laptop scale. Easy questions are solved by one sample and gain little from more; medium questions gain most from cheap selection; on hard questions coverage keeps rising while voting stalls, because the right answer is a minority. Over all 200 questions, 64 (32%) had at least one correct sample among 64 yet lost the full 64-sample vote. Lesson 4's formula says what recovering them takes: a verifier whose false positive rate is small relative to how rare the correct answers are. Note one surprise: bin 5 holds questions with 0 to 2 correct of the first 32 samples (23 of the 40 had none), yet 57.5% of them have a correct answer among the other 32. Zero out of 32 does not mean a rate of zero: bin 5's per-sample rate is 0.041 on the held-out half against 0.017 on the half that chose the bin, and at about 4% per sample, 32 draws usually contain a correct answer. Sorting on noisy estimates pushes unlucky questions into the bottom bin, which is why we held out half.

A scaling harness is three numbers per question and $k$: coverage, what your selection rule achieves, and the gap between them, split by difficulty. The gap tells you how much a better verifier could buy; the bins tell you where to spend the budget.

Exact numbers depend on the model, prompt, temperature and answer parser, and 40 questions per bin give standard errors of several points, so read shapes, not decimals. Extensions to try: add PRM-weighted voting with the process-reward-models course's checkpoint, raise the temperature and watch coverage and voting move in opposite directions, or route each bin to its best method and compare against a single method at the same total number of samples.

blocks.question: In our run, pass@64 was 0.935 and majority@64 was 0.610. A colleague proposes going to 256 samples with majority vote to close the gap. What do you expect?
options: Majority accuracy will rise to about 0.935, since more samples always help voting
pass@k will fall, since more samples add more wrong answers
Little change in majority accuracy: it already flattened (0.540 at k = 8, 0.595 at k = 32), while pass@k keeps rising; a verifier or reranker is needed to close the gap
Majority vote will fail completely at large k
blocks.explain: Voting converges to each question's most common answer; once that is settled more samples change little, as our curve shows from k = 16 on. The questions in the gap need selection that can find a minority correct answer: a verifier, a PRM or tests.

blocks.question: Why did we estimate each question's difficulty from samples 1 to 32 and measure the methods on samples 33 to 64?
options: Using the same samples would make bins partly sorted by the noise in the very samples being scored, biasing per-bin results
vLLM requires two separate batches of 32
Majority vote cannot use more than 32 samples
Samples 33 to 64 were drawn at a lower temperature
blocks.explain: If a question lands in the easiest bin partly because its first samples were lucky, scoring those same samples overstates the bin. Held-out samples give an unbiased read within each bin, as Snell et al.'s cross-validation does for strategy selection.
